title: Attention as prayer
hook: Simone Weil held that attention, taken to its highest, is prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the serenity prayer: serenity, courage, and the wisdom between them. Your line was know the difference. What did you sort yesterday, something to change or something to leave? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

A student sits over a geometry problem and can't crack it. The hour runs out. The page is a mess of crossed-out lines. Was the hour wasted? Simone Weil, a French philosopher deeply drawn to Christ, said no. In an essay written for students, she argued that real effort of attention is never lost, even when the problem stays unsolved. Because what's being trained, she said, isn't geometry. It's attention. And attention, taken to its highest, is the same thing as prayer. Today, that strange and simple claim.

Weil means something specific by attention. Not frowning. Not clenching your jaw. She describes it as more like waiting: holding your own thoughts back, empty and ready, so that what's really there can come in. Straining gets in the way. That's why she cared about schoolwork. A Latin translation, a math proof: done with real attention, she thought, each one stretches the same capacity the soul uses to turn toward God. Then she turns it toward people. Weil wrote that love of neighbor comes down to being able to ask someone, what are you going through? And then actually to look and listen, without rushing to fix them. She thought that kind of attention was rare, and close to a miracle. The Gospel of Luke has a scene she'd recognize. Jesus is a guest in a home. Martha is busy serving. Her sister Mary "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word." Martha complains, and Jesus answers: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part." Readers take this in different ways. Some stress that Martha's work is good too, just anxious. Some hear Mary as a picture of prayer itself. Weil's lens adds one thing: Mary isn't doing nothing. She's attending. A phone buzzing face-down on the table. A friend talking while you plan your reply. A prayer said while thinking about lunch. Weil's point lands on all of them: the opposite of prayer may not be doubt. It may be distraction.

Here's the practice: give full attention to one thing. Settle, and breathe. Choose one sound in the room: a clock, traffic, the hum of a fridge, your own breathing. Listen to it, and only to it. Don't name it or explain it to yourself; just receive it. When your mind slides off somewhere, notice where it went, and come back without scolding. Weil said attention is a kind of waiting, so wait. If you pray, you can let this listening become your prayer, with no words at all. The bell holds the time.
Attention as prayer. Simone Weil's claim that attention, taken to its highest, is the same as prayer: open, waiting, and fully there, for God and for a neighbor.
Your line: attention is prayer. Today, give one person five full minutes. Phone away. Ask what they're going through, and listen all the way to the end. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Some Christians practice prayer as attention, sitting quietly before God without words, or praying while giving full attention to a task or a person; Simone Weil's essays are read in many settings as a guide to this.

match.prompt: attention as prayer — tap the pairs.
pairs: careful and troubled about many things

myth: Weil said real attention means straining as hard as you can
she describes it as a kind of waiting: thoughts held back, empty and ready. straining gets in the way.
Weil thought an unsolved problem can still be worth the effort
the effort trains attention, and she says that is never lost.
in Luke, Jesus tells Martha that one thing is needful
"one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part."

fork.setup: you're sitting at Jesus' feet, listening, while your sister bustles in the kitchen and complains that you've left her to serve alone. what do you do?
options: argue it out in front of the guest.
fork.reveal: Mary stays. when Martha complains, Jesus says Mary "hath chosen that good part." some readers stress that Martha's work is good too.

original.note: French, Weil's language: waiting. she ties attention to waiting; her letters and essays were gathered as Attente de Dieu, in English Waiting for God.

trapdoor: what you thought: prayer means saying words to God.
what it means: for Simone Weil, full attention, open and waiting, is itself prayer, turned toward God and toward a neighbor.
what a scholar hears: Weil ties attention to waiting rather than effort, and treats schoolwork as training: an unsolved problem still trains the soul.

sources.ref: Simone Weil, 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God' (in Waiting for God)

notes: All of Weil is paraphrased (her English translations are not public domain): attention 'taken to its highest' is prayer; unsolved problems still train attention; attention as waiting, not muscular effort; love of neighbor as asking 'what are you going through?'; such attention is rare, close to a miracle. Please check each paraphrase against the school-studies essay.
'A French philosopher deeply drawn to Christ' is chosen because Weil never asked for baptism; confirm the wording is fair.

Original: French 'attente' (waiting) with the title Attente de Dieu; a French word, not a biblical one. Confirm the title and that the note doesn't overstate a link between 'attention' and 'attente' (no etymology is claimed).
Editor pass: the practice changed from looking at a hand, cup or leaf (too close to day 1267's Chesterton practice) to listening to one sound.
Practice outline says 'five minutes'; the sit is two minutes, so the five minutes moved to the carry.

Audit (2026-10-02): no change. Keeper check: the exact 'attention, taken to its highest degree, is the same thing as prayer' wording is usually traced to Weil's notebooks (Gravity and Grace); the school-studies essay says prayer consists of attention. The paraphrase is fair to both, but the source line could add Gravity and Grace.
